blocks.html: on the nature of the question of play & the beginnings of a prehistory of game/play studies

This here represents a first attempt toward manifesting solid a new body fit for a new type of “gamer”. I mean body, of course, in the sense of a body of work I intend to build studiously and up toward magnificence, but also in the sense- in the tradition of all great mysteries- of a body of a Being. A Being which could stand steadfast in the murky waves of our “ludic century”.

At the precipice of the mountain of modernity- scaled quite heroically by our predecessors over the past several hundred years- we encountered a question. The same question at the top of Maslow’s mountain, on the heart of every child, which snakes like a creeping vine through Meinong’s jungle, which lies at the bottom of all philosophical and artistic endeavor as well as mythmaking surrounding technology, and which unites in profound ways the base interrogative instincts of “what?”, “why?”, and especially “how?”. That is: the question of play.

The english word ‘play’ is a powerfully versatile word, used throughout common language in myriad ways within and adjacent to, but also far removed from the context of what we tend to think of as games. Scholars of the topic in our day often focus squarely on the mechanical, creative, and/or the social elements of human play in properly gamic contexts. I hope not to limit my discussions of the topic in any such way. We will later on explore various frames and taxonomies for understanding the landscape of play, but it is important to realize that prior to such structure there is an underlying drive within us towards such a thing in the first place, which I believe ought to be core to our understanding of play as a whole.

Here I’d like to bring the readers’ attention to Roger Caillois’ distinction between “paidia” and “ludus”. Coming from Greek and Latin respectively, the paidiac represents the free play of the child- of the explorer- the ludic representing on the other hand the structured, ruled play of formal games. These two aspects or modes of play are never completely divorced from one another. As any child might attest; primordial, improvised, sandbox-style playing- especially when performed by groups- moves fluidly into temporary structures which emerge through common suggestion or often even unconsciously, (almost supernaturally) guiding and organizing the act of play. We of course see traditional games arise over time, across cultures and between language barriers, through this process of people freely playing together and as is commonly said in the games industry: “finding the fun”. But it is my belief that we can understand this same process at play giving form to what many would, rather than “games” as such, call “institutions”- up to and including academic practice itself. More than just finding fun, this I see as a process of finding meaning in action. I believe it is of crucial importance for those of us attempting to address the question of play to keep this order at the forefront of our minds and remember that truly we are not studying play, but that we are always playing study.

Humans have spent more of our history playing than doing just about anything else we do. It is at our base in a way only comparable to those most fundamental aspects of human identity; tool use, sociality, sense of narrative, and spirituality. Indeed if we take animal play into account it just might predate them all! And if we look broadly at humans’ unique approach to play in games as ritual we might even unite all four under this one umbrella!

Yet, in all this time, for all its significance, just how deeply have we investigated this piece of our picture? Well. Quite deeply actually— if only in scattered niches, many of which remain obscure and under- or completely un-utilized by modern game researchers..

Though games have only come to be understood as a medium comparable to literature, poetry, or cinema and the like through relatively recent developments such as ever-growing prominence and support in university settings through programs like the NYU Game Center, founded in 2008 with a vision to foster an intellectual, scholarly community of research, building on the academic media approach established by Espen Aarseth’s founding of Game Studies in 2001- being the first academic journal dedicated to the study of computer games; analysis of distinctly authored visions of play (a.k.a. most “games”) represents only a small fraction of what might be thought of as the comparably vast field of “play studies”.

Comprised of constellations of flashes in the scholarship of anthropologists, psychologists, educational theorists, economists, theologians, and not least to mention sports scholars; early play studies stretches back to at the very least the work of Stewart Culin, which pioneered a now widely-practiced ethnographic approach to looking at traditional world games near the dawn of the 20th century, a time period which would in its early decades come to see the insights of Johan Huizinga, Marshall McLuhan, Victor Turner, Bernard Suits, Eric Berne, Brian Sutton-Smith, Iona & Peter Opie, Hugo Rahner, and Josef Pieper, among others. These writers would start to reveal in truly erudite fashion the deep ways in which our sacred performances, all media, market behavior, folklore, festivities, and so many other cultural practices have their origin in and continue to engage people everywhere through a basic, curious play.

In the dark of 1943, Hermann Hesse’s Nobel-prize winning Magister Ludi (The Glass Bead Game) would look toward the worlds of future scholarly and artistic pursuit collapsing into a game playing society of a grand scale. And with as many such diversely profound and novel inventions as digital computing, large-scale professional sports, fandom, mathematical game theory, cybernetics, the local arcade, tabletop role playing, the legalization of gambling, and one might even add the very concept of the teenager and shifting perception of “adulthood” invading towns, homes, and consciousnesses everywhere; it is plain to see that society was becoming deeply inoculated with elements of and for play, which was previously more restricted in scope. And which only might be thought to continue growing in influence over human life and culture as material conditions continued to improve. So it makes sense that during this time thinking on play and games was becoming more substantial and (in its own way) revered. But this was all a part of longstanding trends noticed by some far earlier, notably in the work of Cervantes.

Whatever claims might be made to his lucidity, the self-proclaimed knight Don Quixote acts as the first fully ludic man (as well the first practitioner of cosplay!), utterly & inseparably merged with the imaginative play of the romantic virtual worlds of his books, even after (in fact, oddly, especially after) they are lost to him. His playful spirit is of course portrayed as deranged in light of the “serious” and fast changing world around him- maybe somewhat akin to how many might view our modern ludic population: the gamers?-, but a pairing of ludicity and nobility need not be seen as so unhinged or unrealistic. All the way back in 1283, Alfonso X of Castile saw it indeed fit for a king to spend his time creating the Libro de los Juegos (Book of Games), historically marking the first time the rules of chess and backgammon, among other table games, were written down and commented upon. The question of play was also directly asked by St. Thomas Aquinas in the 1485 Summa Theologica which he answers with an affirmation of play’s place in a properly ordered life to ease the tensions of work and suffering. After the manner of knights, kings, and saints, I believe we may find our higher ludic being.

1713’s Essays Upon Gaming by Jeremy Collier raises the question of play boldly in the classical “philosophical” mode of dialogue. And indeed, play runs throughout the works of the great thoughtful dialoguer Plato himself in myriad ways I will surely explore in future writing— to an extent I often like to call Plato the first “paidiosopher”. Philosophy in the sense of creating or putting forward True ideas doesn’t seem to suit the old master; really he seems to resist this quite pointedly. Rather, his work puts Ideas at play with one another; it is in the literary interplay of his many friends, students, and characters each with their own distinct visions and ideas and never quite dictating his own that Plato sees the clearest course towards Wisdom. It is in this sense that it is exactly- beautifully- fit that the history of the study of play is itself found in the interplay of many diverse streams of thought, and betraying this nature would seem to me markedly unwise.

As such, scholars of play should reach always beyond “scholars of play”. We may indulge in the anonymous writer of the Meditations on the Tarot (likely Valentine Tomberg)’s idea that the play of the tarotic Magician represents the foundation of magical and alchemical systems. We may bask in the brilliance of Finnegans Wake, itself I think viewable as a grand ARG of sorts, and which is also at least in part the resulting work of the wordgames and language play that Joyce engaged in endlessly with his equally brilliant daughter Lucia. We may take theories such as Wagner’s “gesamtkunstwerk” or Deleuze’s “rhizome” and find they may have their fullest embodiment in the forms of videogames and metaverses, or find that Heidegger and Tillich’s “ground of all being” might best be conceptualized as a playground!

It is in the spirit of play that we must study play- in the spirit of a gamer that we must study games. And when we do this we find vast horizons of meaning which have been thought by many to lie only in artistic, religious, or intellectual realms. The playful wisdom is distinct from these- though that is by no means to say it is incompatible with them. I hope to pursue these horizons to great length and Paidiasophia (The Wisdom of Free Play) will be a travelog through which I will seek to capture and share new and exotic insights from these far lands, or at least some paths I’ve found out to them. Hopefully that will be helpful to some. And hopefully we’ll have lotsa fun along the way— or it will all be for naught.
